newsitem.title: TAIWAN: U.S. agrees to Taiwan car tariff cut - paper.
newsitem.headline: U.S. agrees to Taiwan car tariff cut - paper.

text.p: The United States has agreed to Taiwan's proposal to cut passenger car import tariffs to 20 percent from 30 percent within nine years after entry into the World Trade Organisation, local media reported on Saturday.
The Commercial Times and Economic Daily News quoted economics ministry officials as saying Taiwan would allow imports of 160,000 U.S. cars in the first year after the island's WTO entry.
Taiwan still needs further talk with European countries about its entry into the WTO after reaching agreement with the United States and Japan, the papers said.
The car quota will grow by 20 percent each following year, with the tariffs being gradually lowered to 20 percent, the papers said.
Officials were not immediately available to comment.
Taiwan hopes to enter the WTO in 1997 but faces an obstacle from rival China which has said it must gain membership first.

Paul Chung, a director of the ministry's Industrial Development Bureau, said in early March that the 20 percent bottom line was a concession from an offer to lower passenger car tariffs to 25 percent five years after WTO entry.
"Despite this our counterparts still are not satisfied," Chung said then. "They want a further cut to 15 percent. We will have to negotiate further about that."
In February, Taiwan lifted a longtime ban on car imports from Japan to conform with WTO's non-discriminatory principles, saying it would allow imports of 7,700 Japanese cars in 1997.

Taiwan would raise the annual quota for Japan to 10,000 cars after its entry into the WTO, officials said at the time. Cars are among one of Taiwan's most restricted industries, with the government maintaining high import tariffs to protect the island's 11 domestic carmakers.
In late 1996, Taiwan agreed to allow the import of 7,000 South Korean cars in 1997, a total that also would rise after Taiwan enters the WTO.
